intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (LCHAD deficiency) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the HADHA gene (600890). paragraphs.text: Long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (LCHAD) deficiency is an autosomal recessive inborn error of mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation (den Boer et al., 2002). Sewell et al. (1994) described it as a newly recognized fatty acid oxidation disorder that is usually fatal. Most patients lack only the LCHAD activity of the mitochondrial trifunctional protein (MTP), and the long-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase and long-chain 3-ketothiolase activities are near normal (IJlst et al., 1996).

paragraphs.text: Tyni et al. (1997) reported 13 patients with LCHAD deficiency, all homozygous for the G1528C mutation. In the first 2 years of life the patients had hypoglycemia, cardiomyopathy, muscle hypotonia, and hepatomegaly. Seven patients had recurrent metabolic crises, and 6 had a steadily progressive course. Two had cholestatic liver disease, which the authors noted is uncommon in beta-oxidation defects. One patient had peripheral neuropathy. Six had retinopathy with focal pigmentary aggregations or retinal hypopigmentation. Dicarboxylic aciduria was found in 9 of 10 patients tested. Some patients had lactic acidosis, increased serum creatine kinase, or low serum carnitine. Three patients had bilateral periventricular or focal cortical brain lesions, and 1 had brain atrophy. Only 1 patient was alive, at 14 years of age, after 9 years of dietary treatment; all the others died before 2 years of age.

paragraphs.text: Jones et al. (2003) grew skin fibroblasts from LCHAD-deficient and normal individuals in medium containing octanoate, decanoate, and palmitate. Adding medium-chain fatty acids reduced the accumulation of long-chain 3-hydroxy fatty acid oxidation intermediates in LCHAD-deficient cells, and decanoate alone worked better than octanoate alone. Over an extended period, a 1:3 ratio of octanoate to decanoate worked best in untreated medium, whereas a 1:1 ratio worked best in medium containing palmitate. The authors noted that all dietary MCT preparations contain more octanoate than decanoate. They suggested that a preparation richer in decanoate may be more effective at reducing potentially toxic long-chain 3-hydroxy fatty acids.

Feeding lowered them by about 60%, and exercise raised them. The authors questioned the usefulness of random outpatient acylcarnitine monitoring and recommended standardized sampling timed to food intake and physical activity. All patients tolerated moderate exercise, which the authors took as support for advising patients to stay physically active.

paragraphs.text: Guffon et al. (2021) retrospectively analyzed 18 French patients (8 female, 10 male) with long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorders, including VLCAD, LCHAD, CACT, CPT II, and MTP deficiencies. The patients were treated with triheptanoin for a median of 22 months (range, 9 to 228 months), and triheptanoin made up 15 to 35% of daily caloric intake. In the year after starting triheptanoin, 10 of 12 pediatric and 4 of 6 adult patients reported less fatigue and fewer, less severe episodes of myalgia. Three patients no longer had severe hypoglycemic events, and 5 of 6 patients who had needed a wheelchair no longer did. Emergency hospitalizations decreased, and no pediatric patient had an emergency hospitalization in the following 12 months. Cumulative annual days of emergency home care fell from 286 to 51. Adverse events were limited to digestive issues that resolved over time. The authors concluded that long-term triheptanoin treatment appeared safe and improved symptoms.
